boccaccio-writing-desk-quiet-room.head: Giovanni Boccaccio was in Florence in 1348, and he later wrote one of the most famous descriptions of that year.
boccaccio-writing-desk-quiet-room.body: Most historians believe that Boccaccio was living in Florence when the great sickness arrived in 1348. A few years later, he began writing the Decameron, a book of one hundred stories. It opens with a long description of the plague in Florence: how it arrived, how people reacted and how the city changed. Historians consider this introduction one of the most important eyewitness accounts of the Black Death in Europe. Boccaccio described what he saw with care and honesty. He also explained that he would tell this sad part briefly, so that readers could move on to the happier stories that followed. Even so, historians read his account carefully. He was a storyteller, and some details may be shaped for effect. Other sources, such as city records and chronicles, help confirm what he wrote. Yet his words remain the clearest picture of how ordinary people in Florence experienced that year.

writer-walking-arno-bridge-sunset.head: In the early 1340s, Boccaccio was called back from Naples to Florence by his father.
writer-walking-arno-bridge-sunset.body: Boccaccio spent his youth in Naples, a lively city ruled by a royal court. There, he enjoyed music, poetry and the company of educated friends. Around 1341, his father's business suffered from the collapse of the great Florentine banks, and Boccaccio had to return to Florence. In his writings, he expressed sadness at leaving Naples, which he remembered as a place of light and happiness. He found life in Florence more serious and less joyful. Historians know about these feelings from his poems and letters. Even so, Florence gave him much material for his stories. He walked its streets and bridges, met all kinds of people and observed their habits. He also studied the works of Dante, the great poet of Florence, whom he admired deeply. Over time, he came to love his city. His later writings show a deep knowledge of its people, places and customs, from rich merchants to humble craftsmen.

tavern-storyteller-listeners-candle-laug.head: Boccaccio collected stories from many sources, including traditional tales told across Europe and the East.
tavern-storyteller-listeners-candle-laug.body: The stories in the Decameron came from many places. Some were old folk tales, told and retold for generations. Others came from French, Latin and Eastern collections. Some were based on real events and people in Florence and Tuscany. Boccaccio reworked them all in his own lively Italian prose. Historians and literary scholars have traced the sources of many of his stories. They show that Boccaccio read widely and listened carefully to the world around him. Taverns, markets and family gatherings were places where stories were exchanged. Storytelling was a popular form of entertainment for all classes. Even so, Boccaccio added much of his own. His characters are vivid and realistic, and his stories are full of humour, cleverness and human feeling. Merchants, priests, craftsmen, servants and noblewomen all appear in his pages. The Decameron gives a rich picture of everyday life and attitudes in fourteenth century Italy.

red-brick-town-certaldo-quiet-street-eve.head: Boccaccio's family came from Certaldo, a small hilltop town built of red brick.
red-brick-town-certaldo-quiet-street-eve.body: Certaldo is a small town in the Elsa valley, about thirty kilometres southwest of Florence. Its old upper part, called Certaldo Alto, sits on a hill and is built almost entirely of red brick. Boccaccio's family came from there, and he spent his final years in the town. He died there in 1375. His house, rebuilt after damage in the Second World War, is now a museum and library dedicated to him. Historians note that Certaldo, like many Tuscan towns, depended on agriculture and trade with Florence. Its streets are quiet, with views over vineyards and olive groves. Even so, the town was part of the wider world of Florence. Families moved between town and city, and news travelled quickly along the roads. Today, Certaldo Alto can be reached by a small funicular railway. Visitors walk its brick streets, see the palace of its former governors and visit the tomb of Boccaccio in the church of Saints Jacopo and Filippo.

old-chronicler-writing-book-study-lamp.head: Giovanni Villani, a merchant of Florence, wrote a great history of his city in the fourteenth century.
old-chronicler-writing-book-study-lamp.body: Giovanni Villani was born around 1276 into a family of Florentine merchants. He worked for some of the great trading and banking companies of the city and travelled widely. According to his own account, he decided to write a history of Florence after visiting Rome in 1300, during a great religious jubilee. Seeing the ruins of ancient Rome, he reflected that Florence, the daughter of Rome, was rising while Rome was declining. His work, called the Nuova Cronica, describes the history of Florence from its legendary origins to his own time. Historians value it as one of the most important sources for medieval Florence. Even so, Villani was not neutral. He wrote as a proud Florentine and a member of the merchant class, and his early chapters contain many legends. Yet for his own lifetime, he provides detailed and often reliable information. He also held public offices in the city and knew its affairs well.

chronicle-manuscript-pages-illuminated-l.head: Villani loved numbers and recorded many statistics about Florence in the 1330s.
chronicle-manuscript-pages-illuminated-l.body: One of the most famous parts of Villani's chronicle describes Florence in the late 1330s, using numbers. He estimated the population, the number of men able to bear arms and the amount of grain and wine consumed. He counted the bakers, the wool workshops, the churches and hospitals, the schools and the children who attended them. He recorded the city's income and expenses. Historians consider this section one of the earliest statistical descriptions of a European city. They use his figures with care, since some are estimates or may be exaggerated. Even so, many details match other records. His description shows a city that was large, rich and well organised. Villani wanted readers to understand the greatness of Florence. His love of numbers reflected the culture of a merchant city, where people kept careful accounts. Today, his chronicle is still read and studied, and his figures appear in many books about medieval Florence.

quiet-garden-twilight-fig-tree-roses.head: Villani continued writing his chronicle until 1348, when he died during the epidemic.
quiet-garden-twilight-fig-tree-roses.body: Giovanni Villani wrote his chronicle over many years, adding new chapters as events happened. In the 1340s, he lived through the collapse of the great banks, which ruined many merchants. He himself was briefly imprisoned for debt. Even so, he kept writing. When the great sickness reached Florence in 1348, he described its arrival. He wrote that the epidemic lasted until, and then left a blank space, intending to add the date later. He died during the epidemic and never filled it in. Historians often mention this unfinished sentence as a reminder of how suddenly the plague struck. His brother Matteo continued the chronicle, and later Matteo's son Filippo continued it again. Historians value the work of the whole family, which covers much of the fourteenth century. Yet Giovanni's own writing remains the most famous. His chronicle preserves the voice of a merchant who loved his city and recorded its life with great care.

tuscan-hills-olive-groves-cypress-farmho.head: Many farmers around Florence worked under a system called mezzadria, sharing their harvest with the landowner.
tuscan-hills-olive-groves-cypress-farmho.body: The countryside around Florence was covered with small farms, vineyards and olive groves. Many farms were owned by families who lived in the city. They let the land to farming families under a system called mezzadria, meaning halving. The landowner provided the land, the house and part of the costs. The farming family did the work. At harvest, the produce was divided, usually half for each. Historians know about this system from thousands of contracts and account books that survive in Tuscan archives. It became especially common in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and lasted until the twentieth century. Even so, the arrangement was not always equal. Farming families often fell into debt to their landlords. Yet the system linked city and countryside closely. City families received wine, oil, grain and fruit from their farms, and farming families had a secure place to live and work. The tidy Tuscan landscape of fields and farmhouses partly grew out of this system.

wheat-harvest-sickles-tuscan-summer-fiel.head: The grape harvest in autumn was one of the happiest times of the farming year in Tuscany.
wheat-harvest-sickles-tuscan-summer-fiel.body: The farming year in Tuscany followed the seasons. In early summer, wheat and barley were harvested with sickles and threshed on open floors. In autumn came the grape harvest, called the vendemmia. Whole families, including children and old people, went out to the vineyards to cut the grapes and carry them in baskets. The grapes were pressed to make wine, which was stored in barrels. Later in the autumn, olives were picked and pressed for oil. Historians know about these tasks from farm accounts, calendars and illustrations in manuscripts. Many medieval calendars showed the labours of the months, with harvesting and treading grapes in September and October. Even so, farm work was hard and depended on the weather. A storm or drought could ruin a harvest. Yet the grape harvest was also a time of celebration. Neighbours helped one another, and there was food, music and the new wine to enjoy when the work was done.

villa-garden-fountain-view-florence-hill.head: Wealthy Florentines owned country houses in the hills, where they escaped the heat of the city in summer.
villa-garden-fountain-view-florence-hill.body: Many rich families in Florence owned villas in the countryside around the city. These houses were surrounded by gardens, orchards and farms. In summer, when the city was hot, crowded and smelly, families moved to their villas to enjoy fresh air, shade and quiet. They supervised their farms, hunted, walked in the gardens and entertained guests. Historians know about villas from surviving buildings, letters and account books. In the fifteenth century, the Medici family built famous villas, but the custom was already well established in the fourteenth century. Even so, villas were not only for pleasure. They were also working farms that supplied the family with food and income. Boccaccio set the frame of the Decameron in such villas, where young people stayed away from the city during the epidemic. Today, many villas still stand on the hills around Florence, among cypress trees and olive groves, with views across the valley of the Arno.

fiesole-hill-view-florence-valley-evenin.head: The hill town of Fiesole, above Florence, is older than the city itself.
fiesole-hill-view-florence-valley-evenin.body: Fiesole sits on a hill about eight kilometres northeast of Florence. It was founded by the Etruscans, an ancient people of central Italy, long before the Romans. The Romans later conquered it and built a theatre, baths and temples there, whose ruins can still be seen. Florence was founded later, as a Roman colony in the valley below, probably around 59 before Christ. In the Middle Ages, Florence grew larger and stronger, and in 1125 it conquered Fiesole. Historians know about Fiesole's history from archaeology and medieval chronicles. Villani described the legendary rivalry between the two towns. Even so, Fiesole remained a pleasant place, with monasteries, villas and wonderful views. Wealthy Florentines built country houses on its slopes. From the hill, the whole city of Florence can be seen spread out in the valley, with the cathedral dome rising above the red roofs. In the evening, the view of the city below is especially peaceful.

summer-1347-wheat-harvest-golden-hills.head: After the hunger of 1346, the harvest of 1347 was good, and bread became plentiful again.
summer-1347-wheat-harvest-golden-hills.body: The years 1346 and 1347 began badly in Tuscany. After heavy rains, the harvest of 1346 failed, and food prices rose sharply. Many poor families went hungry through the winter. The city government of Florence bought grain from distant places and distributed bread to the poor. According to Villani, the number of people receiving bread each day was very large. In the summer of 1347, however, the weather was better, and the harvest was good. Prices fell, and bread became plentiful in the markets once more. Historians know about these changes from Villani's chronicle and from records of grain prices. Even so, the effects of the hungry year lasted. Many people had become weaker, and some historians suggest that the famine may have made the population more vulnerable to disease in the following year. Yet in the summer of 1347, the people of Florence were relieved and hopeful as the golden fields were harvested.

arno-riverbank-summer-evening-swimmers-p.head: On summer evenings in Florence, people gathered along the banks of the river Arno.
arno-riverbank-summer-evening-swimmers-p.body: The Arno was central to life in Florence. It provided water for the wool industry, power for mills and a route for transport. In summer, its banks were busy with people. Washerwomen cleaned clothes on the stones near the water. Fishermen cast their nets. Boys swam in the shallow parts of the river on hot evenings. Historians know about these scenes from stories, city regulations and paintings. Some city laws tried to control swimming and washing in certain places, which shows that these activities were common. Even so, the river could also be dangerous. Floods sometimes swept through the city, as in 1333, when bridges were destroyed and many people drowned. In dry summers, the river ran low and its waters became dirty from the dyeing and tanning workshops. Yet on calm evenings, the riverbanks were among the most pleasant places in the city, cool and lively, with the sun setting behind the hills.

genoese-galleys-harbour-sails-1347.head: Italian merchant ships sailed as far as the Black Sea to trade for silk, spices and other goods from the East.
genoese-galleys-harbour-sails-1347.body: In the fourteenth century, merchants from Genoa and Venice controlled much of the trade between Europe and the East. Their ships sailed through the Mediterranean to Constantinople and into the Black Sea. There, at trading posts such as Caffa in the Crimea and Tana near the mouth of the river Don, they bought silk, spices, furs, grain and slaves brought by caravans across Asia. Historians know about this trade from merchants' manuals, contracts and letters. A Florentine merchant named Francesco Pegolotti wrote a famous guide for traders, describing routes to China. Even so, these long-distance links had a hidden danger. The same trade routes that carried goods also carried disease. Historians believe that the plague spread along these routes from Central Asia to the Black Sea, and from there by ship to the Mediterranean. The busy harbours of Italy, so important for the wealth of its cities, became gateways for the sickness.

caravan-steppe-camels-dusk-distant.head: People in the fourteenth century did not know what caused the plague.
caravan-steppe-camels-dusk-distant.body: Today, scientists know that the Black Death was caused by a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. It was carried mainly by fleas living on rats and other animals, and in some forms it could spread directly between people. This was discovered only in 1894, by the scientist Alexandre Yersin. In the fourteenth century, people had very different explanations. Many doctors believed that disease came from bad air, poisoned by rotting matter or by unusual movements of the planets. Others saw the sickness as a punishment from God for human sins. Historians know about these ideas from medical treatises, chronicles and sermons of the time. In recent years, scientists have studied the DNA of plague bacteria from medieval graves. Their research suggests that the outbreak began in Central Asia in the 1330s or 1340s. Even so, many details remain uncertain. Yet these discoveries have greatly improved understanding of how the disease travelled and why it spread so fast.

ships-arriving-sicily-harbour-autumn.head: In October 1347, merchant ships from the East brought the plague to Messina in Sicily.
ships-arriving-sicily-harbour-autumn.body: According to the chronicler Michele da Piazza, a Franciscan friar, twelve Genoese galleys arrived in the harbour of Messina, in Sicily, in October 1347. They had come from the Black Sea. Soon after their arrival, people in the city began to fall ill. The sickness spread quickly. Historians consider this one of the first recorded arrivals of the Black Death in Europe. From Sicily, ships carried the disease to other ports, including Genoa, Pisa, Venice and Marseille. Within a few months, it had reached many parts of Italy and France. Historians know about these events from chronicles and letters written at the time. Even so, details such as the exact number of ships may not be accurate. Some accounts were written years later. Yet the general picture is clear. Trade routes that had brought wealth to Italian cities now brought a terrible illness, and news of it travelled along the same roads and sea lanes.

venice-harbour-officials-ships-waiting-l.head: In 1348, Venice appointed special officials to protect the health of the city.
venice-harbour-officials-ships-waiting-l.body: When news of the sickness spread, some cities tried to protect themselves. In March 1348, the government of Venice appointed three officials to take charge of public health. They organised burials, controlled the arrival of ships and tried to keep the city clean. Historians see this as one of the earliest examples of a public health authority in Europe. Later, other cities created similar offices. In 1377, the city of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, ordered ships and travellers from infected places to wait thirty days before entering. This was later extended to forty days, called quaranta giorni in Italian, from which the word quarantine comes. Historians know about these measures from city laws and records. Even so, they could not stop the epidemic of 1348, which spread too quickly. Yet the experience led to lasting changes. Over the following centuries, Italian cities developed health boards, isolation hospitals and rules that later influenced public health across Europe.

florence-winter-street-worried-merchants.head: In the winter of 1347 and 1348, news of the sickness reached Florence through merchants' letters.
florence-winter-street-worried-merchants.body: Florence was a city of merchants, and merchants depended on news. Letters travelled constantly between Florence and its business partners in Pisa, Genoa, Venice, Avignon and beyond. In the winter of 1347, these letters began to mention a terrible sickness spreading in Sicily and the ports. Historians know about this from surviving merchant letters and from chronicles. Some letters described the illness and the fear it caused. Even so, people in Florence did not know how close the danger was or how to prepare. City officials discussed measures to keep the streets clean and to control travellers. Some families made plans to leave if the sickness came. Others hoped it would not reach them. Through the winter, life in Florence continued much as before. Shops opened, markets were busy and the bells rang. Yet many people followed the news anxiously, as reports came closer with each passing month.

avignon-papal-palace-rhone-bridge.head: In the fourteenth century, the popes lived in Avignon, in southern France, instead of Rome.
avignon-papal-palace-rhone-bridge.body: From 1309 to 1377, the popes lived in Avignon, a city on the river Rhône in Provence. This period is sometimes called the Avignon Papacy. The popes moved there partly because of violence and instability in Rome and partly because of the influence of the kings of France. In Avignon, they built an enormous Gothic palace, which looked like a fortress. Pope Benedict the Twelfth began it in the 1330s, and Pope Clement the Sixth enlarged it in the 1340s. Historians know about the papal court from its detailed accounts and records. Avignon became a busy international city, full of clergy, lawyers, merchants and artists. Many Italians lived there, including bankers from Florence. Even so, critics called the period a Babylonian captivity, because the popes were away from Rome. In 1348, the plague reached Avignon and caused great loss of life. Today, the Palace of the Popes still stands and is visited by many people.

poet-scholar-study-books-avignon-window.head: The poet Francesco Petrarca, known as Petrarch, wrote hundreds of poems about a woman named Laura.
poet-scholar-study-books-avignon-window.body: Francesco Petrarca was born in Arezzo, in Tuscany, in 1304, to a Florentine family in exile. He grew up near Avignon, where his father worked at the papal court. According to Petrarch's own account, on the sixth of April 1327, he saw a young woman named Laura in a church in Avignon and fell in love with her. Her identity is uncertain, and she may have been married to someone else. For the rest of his life, he wrote poems about her, in Italian, which were collected in a book called the Canzoniere. Historians and literary scholars consider these poems among the most influential in European literature. Even so, much about Laura remains unknown. Some even wondered if she was only a poetic idea. Petrarch was also a great scholar who searched for ancient Latin texts and helped begin the movement later called humanism. He became friends with Boccaccio, and the two men exchanged many letters.

vaucluse-spring-cliff-river-green-valley.head: Petrarch preferred to live in Vaucluse, a quiet valley where a river flows from a spring at the foot of a cliff.
vaucluse-spring-cliff-river-green-valley.body: Petrarch disliked the noise and crowds of Avignon. He called it a place of corruption and wrote harsh words about the papal court. In 1337, he bought a small house in Vaucluse, a peaceful valley east of Avignon. There, the river Sorgue rises from a deep spring at the foot of a tall cliff. Petrarch lived there for long periods, reading, writing and walking in the countryside. He described the valley in many letters and poems. Historians know about his life there from his own writings, which are unusually personal. Even so, he also travelled widely and spent time in Italy. Vaucluse gave him the quiet he needed for study and reflection. Today, the village is called Fontaine-de-Vaucluse, and a small museum stands near the site of his house. The spring remains one of the largest in France, its clear water flowing out of the rock into a green and peaceful valley.

pope-seated-between-two-great-fires-calm.head: During the plague, the doctor of Pope Clement the Sixth advised him to sit between two large fires.
pope-seated-between-two-great-fires-calm.body: Pope Clement the Sixth lived in Avignon when the plague arrived in 1348. His personal doctor was Guy de Chauliac, one of the most respected surgeons of the time. Following the medical ideas of the period, Guy believed that disease spread through corrupted air. He advised the Pope to stay in his chambers and sit between two large fires, which were thought to purify the air. Historians note that this advice may have helped by chance, since fleas avoid heat. Clement survived the epidemic. He also took practical steps. He paid for the dead to be buried, bought a field for a new cemetery and protected the Jewish community of Avignon, who were being falsely blamed for the plague in some places. Historians know about these events from Guy de Chauliac's own medical writings and from papal records. Even so, the Pope could not stop the sickness, which killed a large part of the population of Avignon.

old-manuscript-virgil-handwritten-note.head: Petrarch wrote a note about Laura's death in his copy of Virgil, which still survives in Milan.
old-manuscript-virgil-handwritten-note.body: Petrarch owned a beautiful manuscript of the works of the Roman poet Virgil. It was decorated with a painting by the artist Simone Martini. Petrarch treasured this book and wrote notes in its margins. On one page, he recorded personal events. There he wrote that Laura had died on the sixth of April 1348, during the epidemic in Avignon, exactly twenty-one years after he first saw her. Historians and scholars consider this note very important, because it is one of the few pieces of evidence about Laura. Petrarch was in Italy at the time and learned of her death by letter. Even so, his feelings for her continued in his poetry for many years. The manuscript is now kept in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana, a famous library in Milan. Scholars still study it today. It is a personal link to a poet who lived through the year 1348 and recorded his grief in his favourite book.
